relationships.description: Connects SQL Injection Prevention to api security oauth2 in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: SQL injection (CWE-89) happens when untrusted input is concatenated into a SQL string, letting attackers alter query structure; preventing it requires strict code-data separation via parameterized queries (prepared statements), allowlists for dynamic identifiers, and least-privilege database roles.
spark.keyTakeaway: Never sanitize or regex-escape SQL values—bind every user input through wire-level parameterized queries (`Parse`/`Bind`) and restrict dynamic table/column/sort names to static compile-time allowlists.

concept.whyItMatters: SQL injection remains one of the highest-impact vulnerabilities (OWASP Top 10 A03:2021 / CWE-89) because a single unparameterized `WHERE` or `ORDER BY` clause exposes the entire database—allowing full table exfiltration (`UNION SELECT`), authentication bypass, or OS/file access (`xp_cmdshell`, `COPY TO PROGRAM`) in seconds via automated tools like `sqlmap`.
whenToUse: Every database query across web APIs, background workers, GraphQL resolvers, and internal admin tools that touches user or external input.
Dynamic search, filter, and sorting endpoints where column names or `ASC`/`DESC` directions are chosen by the client (pair prepared statements with strict allowlists).
Stored procedures and dynamic SQL inside PostgreSQL/SQL Server using `EXECUTE ... USING` or `sp_executesql`.
whenNotToUse: Do not rely on regex input blacklists (stripping `'`, `--`, or `UNION`) as a primary defense—encoding tricks and SQL dialect quirks bypass them.
Do not rely on Web Application Firewalls (WAFs) alone; WAFs are a defense-in-depth layer, never a substitute for parameterized queries.
Do not assume an ORM (`Hibernate`, `SQLAlchemy`, `Prisma`) makes you immune—raw query escape hatches (`.raw()`, `text()`, `createNativeQuery()`) reintroduce SQLi if formatted with strings.
keyPoints: Parameterized queries (JDBC `PreparedStatement`, psycopg3 `%s`, Go `db.Query($1)`) send the SQL template (`Parse`) and parameter values (`Bind`) separately at the wire protocol level—data can never become SQL syntax.
Parameters only bind **literal values** (`WHERE email = $1`), NOT identifiers (table names, column names) or keywords (`ASC`/`DESC`); dynamic identifiers require a strict `Map`/`Set` allowlist.
Always apply **least-privilege DB roles**: web app users should never connect as `superuser`, `db_owner`, or `postgres`.
Stored procedures are NOT automatically safe if they concatenate strings internally (`EXEC('SELECT ... ' + @input)`); they must use `USING` or `sp_executesql`.
Defense in depth—PostgreSQL Row-Level Security (RLS), read-only replicas for reporting, and SAST rules (Semgrep/CodeQL)—limits blast radius if a bug slips through.

examples.title: Safe Dynamic Search & Sorting Endpoint
examples.scenario: An e-commerce catalog API accepts `category`, `max_price`, `sort_by`, and `sort_dir` query parameters from users.
examples.outcome: `category` and `max_price` are bound via `PreparedStatement` placeholders (`?`), while `sort_by` is looked up in an immutable `Map.of("price", "p.unit_price", "rating", "p.avg_rating")` and `sort_dir` is validated against `{"ASC", "DESC"}`—completely blocking `ORDER BY (CASE WHEN ...)` blind SQLi.

examples.title: PostgreSQL Stored Procedure & RLS Blast-Radius Reduction
examples.scenario: A multi-tenant B2B SaaS app runs parameterized queries as an `app_writer` role with PostgreSQL Row-Level Security (`CREATE POLICY tenant_isolation ON invoices USING (tenant_id = current_setting('app.tenant_id')::uuid)`).
examples.outcome: Even if a developer forgets a `WHERE tenant_id = $1` filter in a new endpoint, the database engine itself blocks cross-tenant data leakage.

tradeOffs.factor: Server-Side Prepared Statements vs. Client-Side Emulation
tradeOffs.pro: True wire-protocol preparation (`Parse`/`Bind`/`Execute`) enforces strict parser separation and caches query execution plans.
tradeOffs.con: In transaction-pooling proxies (PgBouncer in `transaction` mode), named prepared statements can collide across pooled connections unless configured with protocol-level unnamed statements or PgBouncer >= 1.21 prepared statement support.

tradeOffs.factor: ORM Query Builders vs. Raw Parameterized SQL
tradeOffs.pro: ORMs/query builders (Prisma, jOOQ, SQLAlchemy Core) parameterize values by default and catch schema mismatches early.
tradeOffs.con: Complex analytical CTEs or window functions often force developers into raw SQL methods where accidental f-strings/concatenation can sneak in.

tradeOffs.pro: Mapping user-facing sort keys (`"created"`) to hardcoded SQL identifiers (`"created_at"`) is 100% immune to injection and hides internal column names.
tradeOffs.con: Requires updating the allowlist map whenever a new sortable column is added.

failureModes.name: Second-Order SQL Injection
failureModes.description: User input (e.g., `admin'--` in a username) is safely stored via a prepared statement, then later concatenated unescaped into a background batch or password-reset SQL string.
failureModes.mitigation: Parameterize every query everywhere—never treat database-loaded strings as trusted SQL syntax.

failureModes.name: Unvalidated `ORDER BY` / `IN (...)` Clauses
failureModes.description: Developers parameterize `WHERE` values but interpolate `sort_by` directly or build `IN (${ids.join(',')})` strings.
failureModes.mitigation: Use static allowlists for `ORDER BY` / column names, and native array binding (`WHERE id = ANY($1::int[])` in Postgres) or dynamically generated `?,?,?` placeholders for `IN` lists.

failureModes.name: ORM Raw-SQL Escape Hatch
failureModes.description: Using `User.objects.raw(f"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '{name}'")` or `entityManager.createNativeQuery("... " + name)` bypasses ORM parameterization.
failureModes.mitigation: Pass bind parameters as the second argument (`raw(sql, [name])`) and enforce Semgrep/CodeQL SAST rules banning string interpolation inside SQL calls.

failureModes.name: Over-Privileged Database Credentials
failureModes.description: Application connects as `postgres` or `sa`, turning a read-only injection into `COPY ... TO PROGRAM` remote code execution or `DROP TABLE`.
failureModes.mitigation: Grant only `SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE` on specific tables to the app role; revoke `CREATE` on `public` schema and disable `xp_cmdshell`.

commonMistakes: Escaping quotes with `addslashes()` or `.replace("'", "''")` instead of using prepared statements (vulnerable to multibyte encoding and non-quoted numeric contexts).
Using `LIKE '%' + ? + '%'` incorrectly by interpolating `?` inside quotes (`LIKE '%?%'`) instead of passing `"%" + term + "%"` as the bound parameter.
Assuming `IN (?)` binds an array in MySQL/JDBC—most drivers bind it as a single string unless expanded to `(?, ?, ?)` or using Postgres `= ANY($1)`.
Returning raw SQL exception stack traces (`PSQLException: ERROR: syntax error at or near...`) in HTTP 500 responses, handing attackers schema details.
Forgetting that stored procedures using string concatenation (`EXEC(@sql)`) are just as vulnerable as application-side concatenation.

sections.content:
## The idea

SQL injection happens because a SQL query is a **program** sent as text to a database parser. When an application builds that string by concatenating untrusted user input (`"SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + email + "'"`), the database parser cannot tell where the developer's SQL code ends and the user's data begins. An input like `' OR '1'='1` alters the **Abstract Syntax Tree (AST)** of the query.

**Parameterized queries (Prepared Statements)** eliminate this class of vulnerability by enforcing **structural separation at the wire protocol level** (e.g., PostgreSQL's Extended Query Protocol `Parse` -> `Bind` -> `Execute`, or MySQL's `COM_STMT_PREPARE` / `COM_STMT_EXECUTE`):

1. **`Parse`:** The client sends the SQL template with placeholders (`SELECT id, role FROM users WHERE email = $1`) *before* any user data. The database compiles and locks the AST.
2. **`Bind`:** The client sends the raw user input (`"alice@example.com' OR '1'='1"`) as a typed binary/text parameter.
3. **`Execute`:** The engine compares the literal string against the `email` column—it is **never** re-parsed as SQL syntax.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace how a **Java Spring / JDBC** or **Python psycopg3** search endpoint handles a malicious payload `q = "widget'; DROP TABLE orders; --"` and `sort = "price; DROP TABLE orders"`:

1. **Identifier allowlist check (before SQL):** The API looks up `sort` in an immutable map: `ALLOWED_SORTS = {"price": "unit_price", "newest": "created_at"}`. Since `"price; DROP TABLE orders"` is not a key, the API immediately rejects the request with `HTTP 400 Bad Request`—zero database round-trips.
2. **Wire-protocol `Parse` (valid `sort = "price"`):** The driver sends `SELECT id, name, unit_price FROM products WHERE name ILIKE $1 ORDER BY unit_price DESC LIMIT $2` to PostgreSQL. The planner compiles the AST once.
3. **Wire-protocol `Bind`:** The driver binds `$1 = "%widget'; DROP TABLE orders; --%"` (with `%` and `_` `LIKE` wildcards escaped) and `$2 = 25`.
4. **Safe execution:** PostgreSQL searches literally for product names containing that exact string, returns 0 rows, and never executes `DROP TABLE`. Even if `EXECUTE` were abused, the `app_readonly` role lacks `DROP` privileges.

sections.content:
## Handling tricky SQL constructs safely

Developers often fall back to string concatenation for three specific SQL patterns—each has a clean, safe alternative:

- **Dynamic `ORDER BY` / Column Names:** Parameters cannot bind identifiers. Map user input through a `dict`/`Map` (`{"date": "created_at", "total": "grand_total"}`) and reject unknown keys.
- **Variable-Length `IN (...)` Lists:** In PostgreSQL, bind a single array parameter: `WHERE id = ANY($1::bigint[])`. In MySQL/SQLite, build the placeholder string dynamically using only `"?"` tokens (`", ".join(["?"] * len(ids))`) and pass `ids` as bound parameters.
- **`LIKE` Wildcard Escaping:** Prepared statements prevent SQLi in `LIKE`, but an attacker sending `%%%%` can trigger expensive full-table wildcard scans. Escape `\`, `%`, and `_` in the application before binding `f"%{escaped}%"`.

## SQL injection defense layers compared

| Control Layer | Protects Against | Fails / Bypassed When | Role in Defense-in-Depth |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Parameterized Queries (`Parse`/`Bind`)** | Value injection in `WHERE`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE` | Developer concatenates identifiers (`ORDER BY`) or raw SQL strings | **Primary control** (mandatory) |
| **Static Identifier Allowlists** | Injection in `ORDER BY`, `GROUP BY`, table/column names | Incomplete list or falling back to raw user string on miss | **Primary control** for dynamic SQL structure |
| **Least-Privilege DB Roles + RLS** | Privilege escalation (`DROP`, `COPY TO PROGRAM`, cross-tenant reads) | Does not stop read/write abuse of tables the role *is* allowed to access | **Blast-radius containment** |
| **SAST (Semgrep / CodeQL)** | Catches `f"SELECT ..."` or `+` concatenation in CI before deploy | Obfuscated multi-hop string builders across files | **Automated regression gate** |
| **WAF (ModSecurity CRS)** | Automated `sqlmap` noise and common payloads | Custom encoding, comments (`/**/`), or blind time-based payloads | **Perimeter noise reduction** (secondary) |

## Failure modes

- **PgBouncer Transaction Pooling Collisions:** Older PgBouncer setups in `transaction` pooling mode failed when drivers used named server-side prepared statements (`PREPARE stmt_1`). Ensure PgBouncer >= 1.21 with `max_prepared_statements > 0` or use unnamed protocol-level `Parse`/`Bind`—never disable parameterization by falling back to unsafe string escaping.
- **Blind / Time-Based Exfiltration:** Even when an endpoint returns only `200 OK` or `404` with no DB errors, attackers extract data bit-by-bit using `pg_sleep(5)` or `IF(SUBSTR(...), SLEEP(5), 0)`.
- **Stored Procedure String Concatenation:** Wrapping a concatenated query inside `CREATE FUNCTION` (`EXECUTE 'SELECT ... ' || user_input`) provides zero protection; use `EXECUTE 'SELECT ... WHERE id = $1' USING user_input`.
- **Verbose Error Leakage:** Returning raw SQL error strings in API responses lets attackers map table and column names in minutes.

## Automated verification in CI/CD

Preventing regressions requires automated checks alongside code review:

1. **SAST in Pull Requests:** Configure **Semgrep** or **CodeQL** rules (`java.lang.security.audit.sqli`, `python.lang.security.audit.formatted-sql-query`) to fail builds whenever string formatting touches a DB cursor or ORM raw-query method.
2. **Integration Tests with Injection Payloads:** Include test cases passing `' OR '1'='1`, `"; DROP TABLE users; --`, and `1; SELECT pg_sleep(5)` into search/sort endpoints to verify they return `0` results or `HTTP 400` in `< 50ms`.
3. **DB Role Audits:** Run a periodic CI/migration check asserting that the application DB role has `rolsuper = false`, `rolbypassrls = false`, and no `CREATE` grant on `public`.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Bind 100% of query values using wire-level parameterized queries (`PreparedStatement`, `%s`, `$1`, `@p1`)—including inside ORM `.raw()` calls and stored procedures.
- [ ] Validate all dynamic table names, column names, and `ASC`/`DESC` directions against a hardcoded allowlist `Map`/`Set`.
- [ ] Use `= ANY($1)` (Postgres) or generated `?, ?, ?` placeholders for variable-length `IN` clauses.
- [ ] Connect the application with a least-privilege DB role (no superuser, no `DDL`, no OS command privileges) and enable Row-Level Security for multi-tenant tables.
- [ ] Suppress raw SQL error messages from HTTP responses; log full details internally only.
- [ ] Enforce Semgrep/CodeQL SQLi rules in CI to block accidental string interpolation.

interviewProblems.title: SQL Injection Prevention
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on SQL Injection Prevention. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: SQL injection (CWE-89) happens when untrusted input is concatenated into a SQL string, letting attackers alter query structure; preventing it requires strict code-data separation via parameterized queries (prepared statements), allowlists for dynamic identifiers, and least-privilege database roles.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: DB Driver (Wire Protocol) applies the primary invariant and coordinates with PostgreSQL / MySQL Engine.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, PostgreSQL / MySQL Engine experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Parameterize every query everywhere—never treat database-loaded strings as trusted SQL syntax.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Never sanitize or regex-escape SQL values—bind every user input through wire-level parameterized queries (`Parse`/`Bind`) and restrict dynamic table/column/sort names to static compile-time allowlists.
Avoid trap: Escaping quotes with `addslashes()` or `.replace("'", "''")` instead of using prepared statements (vulnerable to multibyte encoding and non-quoted numeric contexts).
Avoid trap: Using `LIKE '%' + ? + '%'` incorrectly by interpolating `?` inside quotes (`LIKE '%?%'`) instead of passing `"%" + term + "%"` as the bound parameter.
When to reach for it: Every database query across web APIs, background workers, GraphQL resolvers, and internal admin tools that touches user or external input.
When to reach for it: Dynamic search, filter, and sorting endpoints where column names or `ASC`/`DESC` directions are chosen by the client (pair prepared statements with strict allowlists).

putItTogether.title: Putting Sql Injection Prevention Together
putItTogether.summary: Never sanitize or regex-escape SQL values—bind every user input through wire-level parameterized queries (`Parse`/`Bind`) and restrict dynamic table/column/sort names to static compile-time allowlists.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Sql Injection Prevention before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: `category` and `max_price` are bound via `PreparedStatement` placeholders (`?`), while `sort_by` is looked up in an immutable `Map.of("price", "p.unit_price", "rating", "p.avg_rating")` and `sort_dir` is validated against `{"ASC", "DESC"}`—completely blocking `ORDER BY (CASE WHEN ...)` blind SQLi.
